tiles.title: Creating and Inspecting DataFrames
tiles.summary: Build a DataFrame directly from Python data — a dict of lists or a list of dicts — then use head, shape, dtypes, info, and describe to get an immediate overview of what is inside.

steps.title: Two ways to build a DataFrame from Python data
steps.lede: Not every DataFrame starts life as a file. When delivery data already exists as Python objects, you can build the table directly.

blocks.text: Pass a **dict of equal-length lists** to `pd.DataFrame()` and each key becomes a column name; each list becomes that column's values. With no index argument the result uses a default range index: `orders = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [1001, 1002, 1003], "city": ["Lagos", "Abuja", "Kano"]})`.

Alternatively, pass a **list of dicts** where each dict becomes one row and the dict keys become column names: `orders = pd.DataFrame([{"order_id": 1001, "city": "Lagos"}, {"order_id": 1002, "city": "Abuja"}])`. Both routes produce the same kind of table — pick whichever shape your data is already in.

steps.title: Five methods that answer your first questions about a DataFrame
steps.lede: Before doing anything else with a newly loaded or built orders DataFrame, get an overview of what is actually in it.

blocks.text: `orders.head()` shows the first five delivery records by default — a quick sanity check that the data loaded correctly. `orders.shape` returns a tuple of (rows, columns), such as `(250, 10)` for 250 orders across 10 columns.

`orders.dtypes` returns the data type of each column — for example, that `delivery_time_minutes` holds integers and `city` holds text. `orders.info()` combines that dtype list with a count of non-missing values per column and the DataFrame's memory usage in one concise summary.

steps.title: What you learned: creating and inspecting DataFrames
steps.lede: Two construction routes, five inspection tools — here is the summary.

blocks.text: A DataFrame can be built from a **dict of equal-length lists** (one key per column) or a **list of dicts** (one dict per row). Both routes produce the same table — pick whichever shape your Python data is already in.

Five methods answer your first questions: `head()` previews rows, `shape` reports dimensions, `dtypes` lists column types, `info()` adds non-null counts and memory, and `describe()` gives a statistical overview of numeric columns — all in one call each.

remediation_steps.title: List of dicts: each dict is one row
remediation_steps.lede: When you pass a list of dicts, each dict contributes exactly one row.

blocks.text: In `pd.DataFrame([{"order_id": 1001, "city": "Lagos"}, {"order_id": 1002, "city": "Abuja"}])`, the first dict becomes row 0 and the second becomes row 1. The dict keys — `order_id` and `city` — become the column names. Contrast this with the dict-of-lists form, where each key maps to a whole column.

remediation_steps.title: shape vs info() — dimensions vs column detail
remediation_steps.lede: shape tells you how big the table is; info() tells you what is inside each column.

blocks.text: `orders.shape` returns a tuple of (rows, columns) — for example `(250, 10)`. It answers only: how many rows and how many columns? `orders.info()` prints a concise summary that includes column names, their data types, how many non-missing values each column has, and the DataFrame's memory usage. Use `shape` for a quick size check; use `info()` when you need to see missing-value counts.

remediation_steps.title: describe() — one call, many statistics
remediation_steps.lede: describe() computes a statistical overview of numeric columns in a single call.

blocks.text: `orders.describe()` computes a quick statistical overview of each numeric column — count, mean, std, min, 25th percentile, median (50%), 75th percentile, and max — in a single call. It covers all numeric columns at once, so you do not need to call `mean()` and `std()` separately just to get a first look.

tiles.title: Selecting and Filtering Data
tiles.summary: Use .loc and .iloc to select rows and columns by label or position, and apply boolean filters — single conditions or combined with & | ~ — to keep only the rows you need.

steps.title: Two accessors: .loc for labels, .iloc for positions
steps.lede: Pandas gives two different accessors depending on whether you want to address rows by their labels or by their integer positions.

blocks.text: `.loc` selects data **by label** — row index labels and column names. `.iloc` selects data **by integer position**, from 0 to length−1 of the axis. Both accept a row selector and a column selector separated by a comma: `df.loc[rows, cols]`. A colon (`:`) or omitting an axis means 'all of that axis'.

`orders.loc[2:4, "city"]` selects the `city` column for the rows **labeled** 2 through 4 — and because `.loc` uses label slicing, **both endpoints are included** in the result. So `orders.loc[2:4]` returns rows labeled 2, 3, and 4.

blocks.takeaway: .loc includes the stop label; .iloc excludes the stop position — double-check this boundary whenever a slice's last row matters.

steps.title: Selecting rows and columns with .loc and .iloc

steps.title: .iloc uses 0-based positions with an exclusive stop
steps.lede: iloc follows the same slicing rules as Python lists — the stop position is not included.

blocks.text: `orders.iloc[0:3, 0:2]` selects the first three rows (positions 0, 1, 2) and the first two columns (positions 0, 1) by pure position. The stop position 3 is **excluded**, following ordinary Python slicing rules. So `orders.iloc[0:3]` returns exactly three rows — not four.

steps.title: Filter rows with a True/False mask
steps.lede: Suppose you only want the delivery orders that took longer than 25 minutes — a boolean filter does exactly that.

blocks.text: Comparing a DataFrame column with a value — such as `orders['delivery_time_minutes'] > 25` — produces a **True/False Series** of the same length as the column. Passing that Series inside `orders[...]` keeps only the rows where the value is `True`.

When combining multiple conditions, each must be wrapped in parentheses and joined with `&` (and), `|` (or), or `~` (not). For example: `orders[(orders['city'] == 'Lagos') & (orders['delivery_time_minutes'] > 25)]`. Without the parentheses Python evaluates the comparison operators in the wrong order.

steps.title: What you learned: selecting and filtering data
steps.lede: Two accessors and a mask — here is the summary.

blocks.text: `.loc` selects by **label** and includes the stop label in a slice. `.iloc` selects by **integer position** and excludes the stop position, following Python slicing rules. Both accept `[rows, cols]` — a colon means 'all of that axis'.

A boolean filter is a same-length True/False Series you compute first, then pass to `df[...]` to keep only the matching rows. When combining conditions with `&`, `|`, or `~`, each condition must be in parentheses.

remediation_steps.title: .iloc stop position is excluded
remediation_steps.lede: iloc follows Python slicing: the stop is not included in the result.

blocks.text: `orders.iloc[0:3]` returns rows at positions 0, 1, and 2 — **not** position 3. This is the same rule as Python list slicing: `my_list[0:3]` gives three items. Contrast with `.loc`: `orders.loc[0:3]` returns rows labeled 0, 1, 2, **and** 3 — the stop label is included. Always double-check which accessor you are using when the last row matters.

remediation_steps.title: How a boolean mask filters rows
remediation_steps.lede: The mask is a True/False Series — only True rows survive.

blocks.text: `orders['delivery_time_minutes'] > 25` produces a True/False Series the same length as the DataFrame. Passing it inside `orders[...]` keeps only the rows where the value is `True` — every row where the condition is `False` is dropped. The mask must be the same length as the DataFrame's index; pandas aligns them row by row.

remediation_steps.title: Parentheses are required when combining conditions
remediation_steps.lede: Each condition must be in its own parentheses before you join them with & or |.

blocks.text: When combining conditions, each must be grouped in parentheses: `orders[(orders['city'] == 'Lagos') & (orders['delivery_time_minutes'] > 25)]`. Without the parentheses, Python evaluates the comparison operators in the wrong order and raises a `ValueError`. The `&`, `|`, and `~` operators work element-wise on the boolean Series.

tiles.title: Sorting and Renaming
tiles.summary: Sort a DataFrame by one or more columns with sort_values, controlling ascending/descending order per column, and rename column and index labels with rename using a dict mapping.

steps.title: sort_values: sort by one or more columns
steps.lede: Reorder the rows of a DataFrame by the values in one or more columns.

blocks.text: `DataFrame.sort_values(by=...)` sorts rows using the values of the listed column(s). When `by` is a list, the first column sets the primary sort order and each later column breaks ties: `orders.sort_values(by=['city', 'delivery_time_minutes'])` sorts by city first, then by delivery time within each city.

The `ascending` parameter defaults to `True`. Pass a list of booleans matching the length of `by` to sort some columns ascending and others descending in the same call: `orders.sort_values(by=['city', 'delivery_time_minutes'], ascending=[True, False])` sorts cities alphabetically but delivery times from slowest to fastest within each city.

blocks.change_summary: Rows are reordered: city is the primary sort key; delivery_time_minutes breaks ties within each city.

steps.title: rename(): relabel columns and index entries with a dict
steps.lede: Clean up column names or row labels without rebuilding the DataFrame.

blocks.text: `rename()` relabels a DataFrame's axes using a dict mapping (or a function). Pass `columns=` to rename column labels: `orders.rename(columns={'delivery_time_minutes': 'delivery_min'})` renames that one column and leaves every other label unchanged.

A single `rename()` call can rename columns and index labels together by passing both `columns=` and `index=` at once: `orders.rename(columns={'city': 'destination_city'}, index={0: 'first_order'})` relabels one column and one row label in one call — any label not in the mapping is left as-is.

blocks.change_summary: Two column labels are renamed; order_id and all other labels are unchanged.

steps.title: What you learned: sorting and renaming
steps.lede: One method to reorder rows, one method to relabel axes.

blocks.text: `sort_values(by=[...])` reorders rows by the listed columns. The first column is the primary sort key; later columns break ties. `ascending` defaults to `True` and can be a list of booleans to mix directions.

`rename(columns={...})` relabels column headers using a dict mapping; `rename(index={...})` relabels row index entries. Both can be combined in one call — any label not in the mapping is left unchanged.

remediation_steps.lede: To mix sort directions, pass a list of booleans matching the length of by.

blocks.text: `sort_values()`'s `ascending` parameter defaults to `True` (all columns sorted ascending). To sort some columns ascending and others descending in the same call, pass a list of booleans the same length as `by`: `orders.sort_values(by=['city', 'delivery_time_minutes'], ascending=[True, False])` sorts cities A→Z but delivery times from largest to smallest within each city.

remediation_steps.title: rename() with columns= and index= together
remediation_steps.lede: One rename() call can relabel both column headers and row index entries.

blocks.text: `orders.rename(columns={'delivery_time_minutes': 'delivery_min'})` renames one column; every other column label is left unchanged. To rename a column and an index label in the same call: `orders.rename(columns={'city': 'destination_city'}, index={0: 'first_order'})`. Any label not listed in the mapping is untouched.
